stocks.note: Numbers as of market close on July 10th.
stocks.news:
Stocks edged higher to start the week, with all three major indexes in the green. The NASDAQ and the DOW each added 0.29%, to 26,281 and 52,637, while the S&P 500 rose 0.42% to 7,575.

The standout was a chip debut. South Korea's SK Hynix (SKHYV +12.76%) began trading on the Nasdaq on Friday and raised about $25 billion. It is one of the world's largest makers of AI memory chips, the kind that feed Nvidia's (NVDA +4.03%) processors, and demand has been running hot.

The flip side of the AI boom showed up at Amazon (AMZN -0.69%), which announced it is cutting 30,000 jobs, the deepest layoffs in company history, as it restructures around automation. Roughly 40% of companies cited AI as their top reason for layoffs back in May, and Amazon alone plans to spend $200 billion on AI this year.

Up next is earnings season. JPMorgan (JPM), Bank of America (BAC), and Goldman Sachs (GS) all report tomorrow, giving investors an early read on how the economy is holding up behind the scenes.

economy.note: Stocks and the 10-Year as of the July 10th close; gold and silver are spot as of the morning of July 13th; Brent as of July 12th (Market Briefs, Trading Economics, Yahoo Finance).
economy.commentary:
The job market is quietly thinning out. About 720,000 people stopped looking for work in June, enough to pull the headline unemployment rate lower, not because more people found jobs, but because more people left the search entirely. That dragged the labor force participation rate down to 61.5%, near a multi-year low (see today's chart). Fewer people competing for work sounds fine if you already have a job, but a shrinking labor force is usually a sign of caution, not confidence.

There is also a debate brewing over who should share in the AI windfall. In one new survey, 69% of adults said AI companies should hand over half their equity to a government-run sovereign wealth fund, the idea being that as AI profits balloon, some of that gain could help fund public programs.

In the markets, the 10-year Treasury held at 4.57%. Gold slipped about 1.2% to $4,064 and silver fell 1.67% to $58.85. Both came under pressure as fresh U.S. strikes on Iran drove oil higher and revived worries that the Fed may have to keep rates high to fight inflation, which tends to weigh on metals. Brent crude jumped 3.33% to $78.54 after the Strait of Hormuz, which carries roughly a fifth of the world's daily oil, was closed again.

crypto.note: Numbers as of 4:00 PM ET, July 12th.
crypto.commentary:
Crypto drifted lower across the board, with Bitcoin off 1.15% to $63,004, Ether down 1.32% to $1,782, and XRP slipping 0.61% to $1.08.

The bigger news was on the plumbing side. Circle (CRCL +4.97%), the company behind the USDC stablecoin, won federal approval to launch a crypto-focused trust bank, which lets it hold digital assets for banks and large institutions under last year's GENIUS Act. Over time that could bring some of these services to everyday investors.

The AI-trading trend is spreading too. After Robinhood (HOOD) said its AI could buy and sell stocks on a user's behalf, crypto exchange Kraken said it plans to add more AI tools to its app, aiming to make trading simpler at a time when the market is stuck in a rut.

real_estate.homebuilder: Mortgage Rates Hold Near 6.64% As Congress Moves To Ban Big Investors From Buying Single Family Homes; The Median U.S. Price Sits At A Record $440,600; The East Bay Board Climbs To 2,814 Active On 280 New And 179 Closed
real_estate.commentary:
The 30-year fixed held at 6.64% and the 15-year at 6.19%, essentially flat on the week. Rates in this range keep the lock-in effect firmly in place, so most owners stay put and resale supply stays tight.

The policy headline: Congress passed a bill that would bar large investors from buying up single-family homes, a direct swipe at the Wall Street landlords that have scooped up starter homes in recent years. President Trump has not signed it, but if he neither signs nor vetoes within 10 days of passage, it becomes law automatically. For first-time buyers, less competition from deep-pocketed funds could be a small tailwind. The national median existing-home price, meanwhile, is holding at a record $440,600.

Locally, the East Bay board climbed to 2,814 active, up from 2,811, on a busy 280 new listings and 179 closings. Oakland led the board by a wide margin with 72 new on 726 active, followed by Danville at 33 and Fremont at 32.

For agents: rates are stuck, supply is tight, and now there is a policy wild card. If the investor ban becomes law, expect a bit less competition on entry-level homes, which could help the buyers who have been boxed out. Either way, well-priced and well-presented homes still move, so pricing to the comps beats reaching for the record.
